question: What is the primary goal of child growth monitoring in primary health care?

options.A: Providing free meals for impoverished families in the community
options.B: Diagnosing chronic genetic disorders in newborn infants
options.C: Treating children already diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition
options.D: Detecting growth faltering before severe malnutrition appears

explanation: Growth monitoring focuses on early detection so interventions can happen before physical wasting sets in. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: Why is regular weighing more useful than a single weight measurement?

options.A: Single measurements are frequently lost by clinic record keepers
options.B: It shows the direction and velocity of the child's growth
options.C: Mothers only remember weights if recorded multiple times
options.D: National health insurance requires monthly data entries

explanation: A trend reveals whether a child is gaining, stagnating, or losing weight over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: Which growth indicator is most sensitive to acute, short-term nutritional stress?
explanation: Weight fluctuates quickly with sudden illness or food scarcity, making it sensitive to acute changes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: A low height-for-age score in a toddler indicates which condition?

options.A: Wasting from a recent bout of diarrhea
options.C: Normal variation in familial height patterns
options.D: Overweight status due to high carbohydrate intake

explanation: Height deficits accumulate over long periods of poor nutrition or repeated infections, resulting in stunting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: What is the first step before placing an infant on a weighing scale?
explanation: Calibrating or zeroing the scale prevents baseline errors in weight recording. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: Why must a child's shoes and heavy outer clothing be removed prior to weighing?

options.A: To comply with standard hospital hygiene protocols
options.B: To keep the weighing pan clean from mud
options.C: To allow the nurse to inspect for skin lesions
options.D: To prevent false elevation of the recorded weight

explanation: Extra items add unnecessary mass, leading to inaccurate tracking of true body weight. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: How should a child under two years of age have their length measured?

options.A: Lying down on a recumbent length board
options.B: Measured with a flexible tape measure on the floor
options.C: Suspended in a hanging sling scale
options.D: Standing upright against a wall stadiometer

explanation: Infants and toddlers under two cannot stand reliably, so recumbent length is measured instead. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: A nurse measures a three-year-old child using a recumbent board. What should the nurse do next?

options.A: Repeat the measurement standing up with a stadiometer
options.B: Record the recumbent measurement in the child's health card
options.C: Refer the child immediately for developmental delays
options.D: Subtract two centimeters to adjust for standing height

explanation: Children over two years old are measured standing up using a stadiometer for accurate height-for-age comparison. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: What is represented on the horizontal axis of a standard child growth chart?
explanation: The horizontal axis tracks time elapsed, typically measured in months for infants and young children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: What does connecting the plotted weight dots over several clinic visits create?

options.A: A diagnosis of acute infectious disease
options.B: An estimate of adult height potential
options.C: A summary of total vaccine doses received
options.D: A growth curve showing the child's development velocity

explanation: Connecting dots creates a visual trend line that illustrates how the child is growing over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: Which pattern on a growth chart indicates normal, healthy child development?

options.A: An erratic zigzag pattern going up and down
options.B: A sharp downward drop toward the bottom of the chart
options.C: A curve running parallel to the median reference lines
options.D: A completely horizontal line across all months

explanation: A steady upward curve running parallel to reference lines shows consistent and expected weight gain. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: What does a flattened growth curve indicate about a young child?

options.A: Inadequate weight gain or growth faltering
options.C: Rapid recovery from a previous infection

explanation: A flat line means the child has not gained weight since the last visit, which is a warning sign of faltering growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: Which common childhood illness frequently contributes to rapid weight loss and growth faltering?
explanation: Diarrheal diseases lead to nutrient loss and reduced appetite, frequently causing acute weight loss in young children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: Why does recurrent malaria lead to faltering growth in toddlers?

options.A: It permanently damages the bone growth plates
options.B: It directly increases body fat storage while reducing muscle mass
options.C: It suppresses appetite and increases metabolic energy demands
options.D: It prevents the absorption of water in the large intestine

explanation: Infections cause fever and metabolic stress while reducing food intake, tipping the energy balance toward weight loss. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: What is the recommended feeding practice for an infant under six months of age?

options.C: Formula milk mixed with clean water

explanation: Infants under six months need only breastmilk for optimal growth, hydration, and immune protection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)

question: When counselling a mother whose child shows growth faltering, what should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: Advising the purchase of expensive imported dietary supplements
options.B: Giving written lectures on the physiology of metabolism
options.C: Discussing practical meal preparation using locally available foods
options.D: Referring the mother immediately to a tertiary nutrition specialist

explanation: Counselling works best when it offers realistic, affordable dietary changes using foods the family already has. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)
